# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 89 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 89 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_089_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 9, Chapter 6

**1** "And the twelve mountains — what are they?" I asked. "They are twelve peoples dwelling throughout the whole world. To these the Son of God was proclaimed by the apostles." **2** "But why are they different from one another — some rough and rugged, others without plants, others with thorns and thistles, others desert, others with the most verdant grass, others hilly, others smooth, others white — why such diversity?" **3** "Listen," he said. "These twelve mountains are twelve peoples. **4** The first mountain, which was black — these are those who have apostatized and blasphemed the Lord and betrayed the servants of God. There is no repentance for them; therefore they are black, for their kind is death. **5** The second mountain, which had no plants — these are the hypocrites who have believed but bear no fruit of truth. Just as this mountain has no plant and bears no fruit, so these people profess faith but have no fruit of truth in them. Yet they remain capable of repentance, and if they repent quickly, the death that threatens them will not overtake them. **6** The third mountain with thorns and thistles — these are those who believed but became very rich and mingled with the Gentiles. Many thorns and thistles choked out the plants of their faith, so that they no longer bear fruit. These can still come to repentance if they return quickly; but if they delay, they shall die with the godless." **7** "And the fourth mountain with many herbs — the upper part green and the lower part withered — these are the double-minded; they neither live nor are dead, like those who waver in purpose, being neither dead nor alive."

---

### Translator's Note
The twelve mountains typology in Similitude 9 is the most elaborate comparative ecclesiology in early Christian apocalyptic. Mountains 1-4 represent progressively less severe states of spiritual compromise. The "double-minded" (dipsuchos) of mountain 4 is Hermas's recurring diagnosis of the half-committed wealthy. SOPHIA follows LOGOS throughout; PNEUMA's "half-committed" is interpretively helpful but expands beyond the Greek.
